Subject: Treatment of Self-Employed Individuals Under Trump Account Contribution Rules

I respectfully request that Treasury and the IRS consider providing self-employed individuals, including sole proprietors with 1099 income and no employees, the ability to make tax-advantaged employer and/or employee contributions to Trump Accounts for their children.

I am a physician who receives W-2 income from my primary employment and also earn 1099 income through a sole-proprietor consulting business. My W-2 employer does not currently offer a Trump Account contribution program.

Under the current proposed regulations, a self-employed individual is generally not treated as an employee for purposes of the Section 128 employer contribution rules. This creates an unintended disparity between W-2 employees whose employers may establish Trump Account contribution programs and self-employed individuals who have no employer through which to access this benefit.

I encourage Treasury and the IRS to consider allowing a sole proprietor with 1099 income and no employees to participate in a Trump Account contribution program in a manner analogous to the treatment of a self-employed individual under qualified retirement plans. Specifically, self-employed individuals should be permitted to make qualifying employer contributions and, where appropriate, employee contributions to their children’s Trump Accounts with corresponding tax treatment.

Extending this option would provide greater parity between W-2 employees and self-employed Americans, particularly small-business owners and independent professionals, while furthering the purpose of Trump Accounts as a long-term savings vehicle for children.

I respectfully request that Treasury and the IRS consider this issue when finalizing the regulations and provide a clear mechanism allowing eligible self-employed individuals without employees to participate.

Thank you for considering this important issue.

attributes.comment:
To the Department of the Treasury and IRS:

I’m a parent of two young children, and I wanted to take a few minutes to comment on the rules being developed for Trump Accounts.

I’m excited about these accounts and what they could mean for my kids. One of the things I’m trying to do as a parent is give my children a good financial start in life, and I really like the idea of getting money invested for them while they’re young and giving it many years to grow.

There are two things I hope you’ll consider as the program develops.

The biggest one for me is allowing parents to have a financial adviser or broker help manage the account.

I already think about my kids’ savings and investments as part of our family’s overall financial planning. It would make sense to me to be able to have a financial professional we trust help with their Trump Accounts too.

I’m not suggesting that parents or advisers should be able to turn these into trading accounts or start buying individual stocks, crypto, or other speculative investments. I understand why there are guardrails around money that ultimately belongs to a child, and I think some of those guardrails are a good idea.

I just don’t think those protections necessarily mean that parents shouldn’t be able to get professional help managing the account.

If an adviser is managing it, they could simply be required to follow the same investment rules that I would have to follow myself. If I’m only allowed to invest my child’s account in certain types of broad index funds, then my adviser should have to follow those exact same rules.

I’d also like to see parents have a reasonable amount of choice among investments that qualify.

If several different low-cost index funds all meet the requirements for Trump Accounts, I would rather be able to choose among those funds than have every family limited to just one or two options.

For example, I might decide that an S&P 500 fund makes the most sense for my child, while another parent might prefer a total U.S. stock market fund. If both meet the requirements of the law, I think parents should be able to make that choice.

To me, that still accomplishes the purpose of protecting a child’s money. We wouldn’t be picking individual stocks or trying to time the market. We would simply have some flexibility in deciding how our children are invested for the next 15 or 18 years.

I also think this could make parents more likely to continue contributing to these accounts. If I can incorporate my children’s Trump Accounts into the financial planning I’m already doing for my family, I’m much more likely to view them as long-term investment accounts that we keep funding year after year.

That’s ultimately what I hope Trump Accounts become. I don’t want this to just be an account that gets opened because of the initial government contribution and then forgotten about. I’d like it to become one of the tools my wife and I use to help our children build a financial foundation before they become adults.

So my request is pretty simple: please keep the protections for children, but give parents some reasonable flexibility within those protections.

Let us choose among investments that meet the rules, and let us get help from a qualified financial professional if we want it.

I think that would make Trump Accounts more useful to families like mine without changing the basic safeguards Congress intended.

Thank you for giving parents the opportunity to comment and for considering my thoughts.

attributes.comment:
Proposed Sec. 1.530A-3(g)(6) lets a trustee satisfy its monitoring duty with periodic determinations spaced up to twelve months apart, relying on prospectus and public-document review rather than continuous tracking. That interval, paired with the 30-day cure period in Sec. 1.530A-3(g)(5)(ii), sets up a timing problem the preamble does not resolve: Sec. 1.530A-3(g)(5)(ii)(B)(1) states that when a trustee is out of compliance with its own monitoring schedule, an investment fund is deemed to have ceased being an eligible investment "on the first day" it stopped qualifying, not on the day the trustee actually notices. If a trustee misses a periodic check, the 30-day clock has already been running, in some cases already expired, before anyone catches the problem.

The consequence lands entirely on the account beneficiary, who is a minor with no role in trustee compliance. Under Sec. 1.530A-3(g)(3), missing the cure window converts the account's entire fair market value into a deemed distribution and terminates its status as a Trump account and as an IRA under 26 U.S.C. 408(a). A trustee's late paperwork becomes the child's taxable event. Fixing this does not require abandoning the 30-day standard, which the preamble defends as balancing promptness against orderly trading; it requires running that 30 days from the date of actual discovery, or from the next scheduled periodic determination, when the trustee's own monitoring lapse is what delayed discovery in the first place.

A second gap concerns cost. Section 530A(b)(3)(A)(iii) caps an eligible investment's annual fees and expenses at 0.1 percent of the account balance, and the preamble in Part IV of the Explanation of Provisions states plainly that this cap "does not apply to trustee fees" — custodial and account-level charges are analyzed separately, with no proposed ceiling at all. The preamble even invites comment on "the possibility of prohibiting trustees from charging any fees," which is a tell that the current draft leaves the door open to exactly the outcome section 530A was written to prevent: a compliant, cheap index fund sitting inside an account that a trustee otherwise drains through account-level charges. Congress capped the fund-level fee at 0.1 percent because fee drag compounds over the roughly seventeen-year holding period the growth-period definition contemplates; a rule that caps one fee layer and leaves the other unbounded does not achieve that purpose. A specific numerical trustee-fee ceiling, or at minimum a firm deadline for resolving the open comment request, would close this before final adoption rather than after account balances are already affected.

A third, narrower point involves the ESG exclusion in proposed Sec. 1.530A-3(e)(3), adopted under the residual "other criteria" authority in section 530A(b)(3)(A)(iv). That authority carries no textual limit tying it to the statute's fungibility or index-tracking purpose, so the same clause used here to exclude ESG-tracking funds could, in later guidance, add or remove other fund categories with no comparable public explanation. Anchoring any future use of that authority to a defined nexus with tracking, leverage, or cost — the three criteria section 530A(b)(3)(A) actually specifies — would prevent the residual clause from becoming an open-ended eligibility switch.

A fourth point concerns the administrative-error correction procedure in proposed Sec. 1.530A-3(g)(7), which requires a trustee to sell and reinvest misallocated assets within 30 days of an oversight or mistake in applying its own procedures, and separately notes that Treasury and the IRS "are considering" a rule to let a trustee restore lost earnings without the restoration counting as a contribution subject to the annual limit. Leaving that restoration mechanism as a request for comment rather than a proposed rule means the correction procedure currently addresses only principal, not the growth that principal would have earned during the error period — a gap that, for a long holding period account, can matter more than the error itself. Adopting the earnings-restoration concept in the same rulemaking that finalizes the correction procedure, rather than deferring it, would close the gap the preamble has already identified but not yet filled.

These are gaps in an otherwise workable implementation of a new statutory scheme, not objections to the scheme itself; the underlying eligible-investment framework, including the 90 percent U.S.-company safe harbor and the default-investment mechanism, tracks the statute's text closely. The timing, fee-cap, and earnings-restoration gaps above are the parts most likely to produce an outcome contrary to what section 530A was designed to protect: a child's long-term, low-cost savings.

attributes.comment:
I support the investment guardrails established by this proposed rule. Because Trump Accounts are intended to provide children with a long-term financial foundation, I believe it is important to protect these funds from unnecessary risk, excessive fees, and highly speculative investment decisions during a child's formative years.
Limiting eligible investments to low-cost mutual funds and ETFs that track broad market indexes is a reasonable approach. Broadly diversified index funds can provide children with exposure to long-term market growth while reducing the risks associated with concentrating their savings in individual stocks or other more speculative assets.
I also strongly support the proposed 0.10% cap on annual fees and expenses. Even relatively small differences in investment fees can have a meaningful impact when money is invested and compounded over the years. Keeping fees low helps ensure that more of the account's investment growth ultimately benefits the child rather than being lost to investment-management expenses.
Finally, I support applying these investment restrictions during the child's growth period rather than permanently. The purpose of these guardrails should be to protect the child's assets while the child is a minor, not to unnecessarily restrict the individual's investment choices later in life. Once the beneficiary reaches adulthood and assumes greater responsibility for the account, they should have greater freedom to determine how their money is invested based on their own goals, circumstances, and tolerance for risk.

Re: Guidance on Eligible Investments for Trump Accounts, CC-00349938-26

I am a Muslim parent. I support giving children access to low-cost, diversified investments. I also have religious concerns about where those investments go. Families should have a practical way to participate without investing in businesses that conflict with their faith.

Please revise proposed §1.530A-3(e)(2) to distinguish a sector-concentrated index from a diversified index that applies religious exclusions across industries. Excluding alcohol, gambling or conventional interest-based finance does not by itself establish that an index targets a particular sector. Please evaluate diversification and concentration directly, and explain how business-activity exclusions and financial-ratio screens are treated.

Please also clarify under (e)(3) that religious screening alone does not make an index an ESG index. Fund eligibility should turn on the actual methodology and applicable requirements. Treasury should assess whether the combined provisions leave religiously observant families without a usable investment option, and consider accommodations consistent with the statute. Aggregate demand for ESG funds does not answer that participation question.

I recognize that Congress imposed a 0.10% annual fund-fee-and-expense ceiling and other index requirements. I am not requesting that Treasury disregard those limits. Please provide worked examples explaining how a religiously screened fund could satisfy all requirements, including the qualified-index futures condition, and how a qualifying low-cost share class or disclosed expense waiver would be assessed. Where statutory requirements prevent a workable option, please identify the obstacle and the legislative change needed.

Please preserve and strengthen responsible-party choice under (g)(4). Parents should be able to choose among qualifying funds, allocate across them, and provide continuing instructions for contributions and reinvestment of fund dividends and distributions. Please consider requiring trustees to disclose their available funds and offer a practical process for requesting an additional eligible fund. Families should receive advance notice of investment changes where feasible, and trustees should honor lawful standing instructions when replacing an investment.

Please also address trustee and transaction fees so that the fund expense ceiling does not become a low-cost label on an expensive account. Clear disclosures and affordable access matter especially for small balances.

My requested outcome is a low-cost, diversified option that families can select and manage consistently with their religious commitments. Please explain whether broader parent-directed stock purchases would require legislation or could be addressed under existing authority in a separate rulemaking. Meaningful family choice should guide both this rule and any future legislation.

I request that the Department of the Treasury and Internal Revenue Service reconsider the proposed investment regulations under 26 CFR § 1.530A-3 insofar as they permit automatic investment of funds in accounts established for minor children without affirmative parental authorization.

My objection is not to the availability of voluntary investment opportunities for children. It is to the combination of government-initiated account creation, restricted investment choices, and the absence of an identified procedure through which a parent or legal guardian may decline participation.

I request that Treasury:

1. Explain its statutory authority to direct investments in an automatically established account over an express parental objection.
2. Establish a procedure for parental notification and objection before funds are invested.
3. Explain whether the statute permits capital-preservation alternatives and, if not, identify the statutory limitation.
4. Disclose how default investments are selected, who exercises shareholder voting rights, and what protections address conflicts of interest.
5. Reconsider the proposed regulations and defer their finalization until these concerns have been addressed.

I further request that Treasury consider these objections in conjunction with the September 30, 2026 regulations governing automatic enrollment, because the investment restrictions and nonconsensual account-creation procedures operate together.

The availability of a government-sponsored financial benefit should not be treated as equivalent to affirmative parental authorization for investment decisions involving a minor child.

As an American taxpayer, I support helping children build financial security. However, I believe the public deserves greater transparency about how the financial institutions involved in Trump Accounts are selected and monitored.

Before these investment rules are finalized, I respectfully ask the Treasury and IRS to address the following questions:

1. How are investment funds selected? What standards ensure that decisions are made in the best interests of children rather than financial institutions or political interests?
2. Who benefits financially? Will all fees, compensation agreements, and financial benefits to participating institutions be publicly disclosed?
3. How are conflicts of interest prevented? What safeguards ensure that government officials, financial institutions, and politically connected individuals cannot improperly influence investment decisions?
4. Who controls shareholder voting rights? What protections prevent these investments from being used to influence corporations for political purposes?
5. Who provides independent oversight? Will the public receive regular reports showing where the money is invested, what fees are charged, and whether the program is benefiting children as intended?

I am not alleging wrongdoing. I am asking for clear answers and meaningful safeguards before these rules are finalized.

Regardless of political affiliation, Americans deserve transparency and accountability when taxpayer dollars are involved.

Public trust should be earned through openness, not assumed.

Re: Guidance on Eligible Investments for Trump Accounts (IRS and CC-00349938-26; Docket IRS-2026-1090; RIN 1545-BS14; FR Doc. 2026-17123, 91 FR 54280, August 21, 2026)

To the Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service:

I am a private citizen in California commenting on my own behalf.

I support Trump Accounts and I support this proposal. The law already points these accounts in the right direction: only mutual funds or ETFs that track an index of mainly U.S. stocks that is not limited to one industry or sector, with no leverage and total annual fees and expenses of no more than 0.1 percent. Treasury estimates the rules will affect 85 million children in 44 million families. With small starting balances and many years to grow, low costs and simple, safe choices matter a great deal. I respectfully ask Treasury and the IRS to:

1. Keep the fee cap broad. I support counting every fee a fund charges, including sales loads and redemption fees, no matter what it is called. As the preamble says, any carve-out would push funds to charge fees in that form.

2. Count fee waivers only if they last. A fund should not qualify because of a temporary waiver it can end soon after families buy in. Only contractual waivers or reimbursements disclosed in the prospectus that run at least until the trustee's next yearly review should count toward the 0.1 percent cap.

3. Keep trustee fees at zero, or close to it (Part IV). I support the idea of barring trustees from charging fees on the account or its investments during the growth period. If some fees are allowed, they should be capped, shown in dollars as well as percentages, and never charged for opening or closing an account or for moving it to another trustee. Trustees should not require families to buy advice or other products to get an account.

4. Make the default investment a broad, low-cost U.S. index fund. Many families will never change the default, so it should be a broad market fund, such as one tracking the S&P 500 or a total U.S. market index, at one of the lowest costs the trustee offers. It should be clearly disclosed, as the proposal requires.

5. Keep risky products out. I support the proposal's exclusion of actively managed, leveraged, and sector funds and of any fund that tries to perform differently from its index, and its focus on the risk of the fund as a whole. Please keep these limits firm as new fund types appear, so these accounts are never used to sell complex or costly products to parents.

6. Make children whole after trustee mistakes. I support the rule Treasury is considering to let a trustee restore earnings lost through its own administrative error, without counting that as a contribution. Children should not bear the cost of a trustee's mistake.

7. Use plain language. Notices after a fund is sold and replaced, and error notices, should say in plain words what was sold, what was bought, why, and any cost to the account. Trustees should show the total yearly cost of each fund they offer in one simple table.

8. Let donated stock build ownership, then diversify (Part III). I support allowing gifts of publicly traded stock. Children could hold donated shares for a limited time, such as up to five years, so they truly own a piece of an American company. After that, the shares should move into the account's eligible index fund on a fixed schedule set by Treasury, not by the donor. No single company's stock should exceed a set share of any account, and donors should have no say over when shares are sold or which children receive them.

For policymakers more broadly: enrollment should stay simple, with the $1,000 pilot contribution reaching every eligible child with as few steps for parents as possible. Over time, Trump Accounts could also become a natural channel for any future U.S. sovereign wealth fund or citizen dividend that Congress might create, and I would welcome a study of that idea.

Thank you for this work and for the chance to comment.

Respectfully,
Alec Snelling
California

This comment was crafted with super intelligence (SI) support.

attributes.comment:
Heir Command, LLC submits the attached comments on the proposed regulations governing eligible investments for Trump accounts.

A disclosure can be sent without ever reaching the person it was intended to inform. A notice describing an event that has already occurred can fail silently, particularly where the account belongs to a child and the legally responsible adult is unreachable or unaware.

The proposed regulations establish four disclosure requirements concerning accounts held for minor children. Two describe standing investment arrangements and two report events after they have occurred. The rule does not specify how a disclosure must be delivered, what address a trustee must use, what a trustee must do when a disclosure is returned undelivered, or what evidence of a failed delivery must be retained. The words undeliverable, returned mail, last known address, locate, missing, unclaimed, escheat, abandoned, and lost do not appear anywhere in the document.

The burden estimate confirms the concern. The disclosure provisions are priced under the heading “Sending disclosure notice,” at one minute per response. That estimate measures transmission without separately accounting for address verification, returned notices, or documenting delivery failures.

Sent is not received. A completed disclosure process must make known delivery failures visible and require documented follow-up.

The attached comments recommend a delivery standard, a required response to undeliverable disclosures, retention of transaction-level notification records, and burden estimates reflecting the obligations actually imposed. Proposed regulatory language is included for each.

Heir Command, LLC respectfully requests that the Treasury Department and the Internal Revenue Service schedule a public hearing on these proposed regulations.

attributes.comment:
Must consist entirely of equity investments in primarily U.S. companies (with a 90% weighting safe harbor). Sector-specific indices and ESG indices are disqualified under the Secretary's discretionary authority because they limit exposure in a manner similar to sector funds.

Families should be able to choose among eligible, low-cost investments that meet appropriate financial safeguards. The fact that an index considers ESG factors does not, by itself, establish that a fund is excessively expensive, uses leverage, or fails to track its stated benchmark. The proposed rule should distinguish between the objective financial characteristics of a fund and the considerations used to select the companies included in its index.

The proposal’s discussion of economic effects suggests that excluding ESG funds would have little overall impact because these funds represent a relatively small share of the broader investment market. However, the size of a market segment does not establish that excluding it is justified. For families who wish to invest according to particular financial, environmental, or social considerations, this restriction would eliminate options they might otherwise consider suitable for their children’s long-term savings.

I ask the Treasury Department and IRS to:

Remove the categorical ESG exclusion and assess investment funds using consistent, objective eligibility criteria.

Explain the statutory and evidentiary basis for this additional restriction, including why ESG-related criteria warrant separate treatment from other index-selection methodologies.

Consider less restrictive alternatives that preserve safeguards against excessive fees, leverage, and unsuitable investments without unnecessarily limiting family choice.

Strengthen protections against account-level fees. The proposal itself requests comments on whether trustee fees should be prohibited. The agencies should consider prohibiting or tightly limiting these charges and requiring clear disclosure of all costs borne by beneficiaries. Fees can reduce the value of savings over a child’s investment period, making meaningful cost protections especially important.

Trump Accounts are intended to support long-term savings for children. Their rules should prioritize children’s financial interests, transparency, reasonable costs, and access to a range of suitable investments. A categorical exclusion based on ESG criteria is not necessary to achieve those goals if funds can instead be assessed against clear, consistently applied standards.

I respectfully request that the Treasury Department and IRS revise the proposed regulations to remove the blanket ESG-index exclusion and adopt an approach that protects beneficiaries without unnecessarily restricting their investment options.

attributes.comment:
"The Treasury Department and the IRS intend to exercise regulatory authority conferred by section 530A(a) to issue regulations that would allow contributions of readily tradable public company stock to be made to Trump accounts as part of a philanthropic contribution."
This is not allowed by section 530A(a). 530A(a) specifically refers to the taxable *treatment* of the account, not the holdings therein.
(a) General rule
Except as provided in this section or under regulations or guidance established by the Secretary, a Trump account shall be treated for purposes of this title in the same manner as an individual retirement account under section 408(a).

The specific statutory requirements for eligible investments are listed in given in 530A(b)(3), and cannot be overruled or ignored by regulations or guidance established by the Secretary, see, e.g., Social Security Bd. v. Nierotko (1946); SAS Institute Inc. v. Iancu (2018). The general introductory clause cannot be used by an agency to nullify a specific, mandatory prohibition found elsewhere in the same law.

A donation by a philanthropic individual could be transferred to the Treasury Department as proposed, and then the Treasury Department could give an equivalent deposit to eligible accounts to be invested in eligible investments. However, the Treasury Department would need to do due diligence to determine if it has Budget Authority to grant the secondary gift to the individual accounts, as typical gifting to the government is defined under 31 U.S. Code § 3113, which is specific for reducing Federal debt.

Treasury has claimed in its temporary regulations (RIN 1545-BS27; Treasury Decision 10056; https://public-inspection.federalregister.gov/2026-20026.pdf) that "holding qualified stock received pursuant to a qualified stock contribution does not violate this restriction because no funds in the account are used to acquire the contributed stock". The Secretary argues that Section 530A only bans the active transaction of buying individual stock, not the passive holding of it. Yet, in Proposed § 1.530A-3(g)(5)(ii), the Secretary openly recognizes that an account cannot continuously hold an asset that is non-compliant. If the continuous holding of a disqualified index fund is a disallowed investment, then the continuous holding of an individual corporate stock is equally a disallowed investment. The Treasury cannot claim 'investing' is instantaneous for corporate donations but continuous for index funds.

attributes.comment:
Exclusion of ESG indices under the authority of 530A(b)(3)(A)(iv) is arbitrary and capricious, and in likely violation of the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, 42 U.S.C. § 2000bb-1 et seq. ("RFRA"). See, e.g., Heritage Foundation, comment IRS-2026-1090-0039. RFRA prohibits the government from substantially burdening a person’s exercise of religion unless the government demonstrates that the burden arises from a compelling governmental interest and is the least restrictive means of furthering that interest. Here, the Treasury’s stated rationale for the exclusion is that "it is appropriate to exclude investment funds that track ESG indices because they limit exposure to companies in a way that makes them similar to sector-specific funds." However, as the Treasury has conceded, ESG funds are not sector-specific funds, and ALL managed funds limit exposure as they deem appropriate. Additionally, Treasury also notes that "ESG investing returns were generally indistinguishable from conventional investing returns". The Department cannot simply brush aside the economic reality that "ESG" is not a monolith, but a broad spectrum of data points used by sophisticated actors to navigate risk. By targeting these indices based solely on their classification, the Treasury is making a decision that is untethered to the actual economic function of the funds. Treasury proposes "an ESG index includes any index that has, or is marketed as having, a focus on environmental, social, or governance factors." Any regulatory action that excludes a fund solely based on its descriptive terminology is an arbitrary and capricious use of administrative power. Furthermore, if the Department’s objective is to ensure diversification, it could achieve that goal through less restrictive regulatory measures such as imposing specific concentration limits on indices.

The proposed rule constitutes a substantial burden on the religious exercise of many Americans, violating the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA). For many religious practitioners and faith-based organizations, the management of capital is an extension of their religious observance. Many denominations utilize ESG criteria to ensure their investments do not support activities that contradict their tenets, such as exploitative labor practices, certain weapons manufacturing, or environmental degradation (often framed as "creation care"). By banning access to these indices writ large, the Treasury Department effectively strips observant families of tools to align their financial lives with their deeply held religious convictions. This forced choice between participating in legally authorized ways to build capital for our children's financial futures and adhering to religious mandates regarding stewardship and ethical conduct imposes a substantial burden on the religious exercise of citizens.

Heritage Foundation, comment IRS-2026-1090-0039, suggests excluding ESG funds but allowing faith-based or values-based funds. However, this risks violating the principle of religious neutrality by creating a preferential classification for "faith-based" investments. The investment approach of these different funds are largely indistinguishable from many ESG funds, and as previously noted, excluding a fund based on its descriptive terminology is arbitrary and capricious. A regulatory framework that exempts indices branded as "faith-based" while penalizing secular indices that utilize the same environmental, social, and governance metrics constitutes an impermissible government endorsement of specific religious identities.

attributes.comment: HEIR COMMAND, LLC requests that Michelle Wilner, Founder and Chief Executive Officer, be scheduled to testify for 10 minutes at the December 16, 2026 public hearing on Guidance on Eligible Investments for Trump Accounts, CC-00349938-26. The attached request and outline address a narrow question: how should trustees document whether required investment-related notices and disclosures were delivered, failed, or have an unknown delivery outcome? The testimony will recommend a technology-neutral recordkeeping standard that preserves those distinctions without treating delivery as proof that a recipient read or understood a notice, and without delaying any investment correction or reinvestment. The testimony will also address reasonable follow-up after known delivery failures, confidentiality safeguards, and implementation burden. Please see the attached PDF for the complete outline and time allocations.
